mcq.q: How do Parasuraman and Riley (1997) define "automation"?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: concepts and context
o: The performance by a human of a new function that no machine had ever been able to carry out before
The replacement of all operators by machines so that a system runs without any supervision at all
The execution by a machine agent (usually a computer) of a function that was previously carried out by a human
The ability of machines to redesign themselves to perform functions their designers never imagined
mcq.e: The paper: "We define automation as the execution by a machine agent (usually a computer) of a function that was previously carried out by a human."

mcq.q: Why does what counts as "automation" change over time?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: concepts and context
o: Because safety law requires every device to be re-registered as automation after every ten years of operation
Because researchers often rename old devices with new names so that papers look newer to their readers
Because every automated system is gradually replaced by manual control after a long period of use
When a reallocation of a function from human to machine is complete and permanent
mcq.e: The paper: "When the reallocation of a function from human to machine is complete and permanent, then the function will tend to be seen simply as a machine operation, not as automation" (e.g., starter motors, automatic elevators).

mcq.q: According to the paper, how does automation affect human work?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: concepts and context
o: It does not supplant human activity but changes the nature of the work
It always makes human work lighter and simpler, so operators gain extra time to rest
It has no effect on human work because machines and humans do two entirely separate jobs
It always fully replaces human activity, so the operator's job largely disappears from the system
mcq.e: The paper: "automation does not supplant human activity; rather, it changes the nature of the work that humans do, often in ways unintended and unanticipated by the designers of automation."

mcq.q: How does the paper describe levels of automation?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: concepts and context
o: As three fixed levels of low, medium and high, and each system must fit exactly one of them
As a continuum of levels rather than all-or-none; Sheridan (1980) identified 10 levels
As two separate states: fully manual or fully automatic, with nothing in between the two
As a fifteen-level scale set by Riley (1989) based on installation cost and time
mcq.e: The paper: "Automation can be usefully characterized by a continuum of levels rather than as an all-or-none concept... Sheridan (1980) identified 10 such levels of automation".

mcq.q: Under full automation, what does the human operator see?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: concepts and context
o: All internal operations, and can override any processing step at any time
All feedback on the machine's intentions, with the right to approve every action it takes
Only the products of the function, not its internal operations
Nothing at all, because the system is completely hidden and has no display for the operator
mcq.e: The paper: "the machine controls all aspects of the function, including its monitoring, and only its products (not its internal operations) are visible to the human operator."

mcq.q: According to the paper, what were the primary criteria for applying automation until recently?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: concepts and context
o: Training results and the satisfaction of the operators
Technological feasibility and cost
The needs and abilities of the humans who will run the system
Safety regulations in each individual country
mcq.e: The paper: "Until recently, the primary criteria for applying automation were technological feasibility and cost."

mcq.q: What does the paper (by its own statement) focus on?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: concepts and context
o: The influence of automation on the performance of whole organizations
The influence of automation on the behavior of entire work teams
The influence of automation on social and political structures
The influence of automation on individual task performance
mcq.e: The paper: "We focus on the influence of automation on individual task performance. We do not consider in any detail the impact of automation on team or job performance or on organizational behavior".

mcq.q: How are the terms misuse, disuse and abuse used, according to the paper?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: concepts and context
o: As three legal charges that courts use to assign blame to pilots after accidents
As ways of blaming managers for deliberately sabotaging the company's automated systems
With no pejorative intent toward operators, designers, managers or regulators
As names for deliberate errors that only operators can commit during a shift
mcq.e: The paper: "in using terms such as misuse, disuse, and abuse, no pejorative intent is implied toward any of these groups."

mcq.q: How does the paper define "misuse"?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: concepts and context
o: Designers applying automation without considering consequences for human performance
Overreliance on automation, e.g., using it when it should not be used or failing to monitor it effectively
Ignoring or underusing automation, such as turning off a device's automated alarms
Turning automation on according to procedure and monitoring it closely throughout the shift
mcq.e: The paper: "We define misuse as overreliance on automation (e.g., using it when it should not be used, failing to monitor it effectively)".

mcq.q: How does the paper define "disuse"?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: concepts and context
o: Inappropriate application of automation by designers or managers in an organization
Overreliance, e.g., using it when it should not be used and failing to monitor the system well
Voluntary switching of automation on and off according to the operator's needs at the time
Underutilization of automation, e.g., ignoring or turning off automated alarms and safety systems
mcq.e: The paper: "disuse as underutilization of automation (e.g., ignoring or turning off automated alarms or safety systems)".

mcq.q: How does the paper define "abuse"?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: concepts and context
o: Operators trusting the machine too much and ceasing to monitor other cockpit information
Operators using the machine for the wrong purpose to gain some personal benefit on duty
Operators taping over or disabling warning devices so they are not disturbed while working
Designers or managers applying automation without due regard for consequences for human performance
mcq.e: The paper: "abuse as inappropriate application of automation by designers or managers (e.g., automation that fails to consider the consequences for human performance in the resulting system)".

mcq.q: How does the paper define "use"?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: concepts and context
o: The machine switching between operating modes by itself, without the operator
The manager forbidding or allowing use of automation in the organization
The voluntary activation or disengagement of automation by human operators
The designer adding a new function to the company's system
mcq.e: Abstract: "Use refers to the voluntary activation or disengagement of automation by human operators."

mcq.q: Which concept does the 1987 accident near Baltimore illustrate?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: concepts and context
o: Abuse: designers removed all warning functions from the cab to save cost
Misuse: crews trusted the system too much and did not watch signals outside along the track
Disuse: inspectors found crews taping over the buzzers that warned of speed violations
Use: crews voluntarily engaged the automatic system according to rules before departure
mcq.e: The paper: "Underreliance on automation was demonstrated in railroad accidents... inspectors found that the train operators were continuing to tape over the buzzers that warned them of speed violations".

mcq.q: Which concept does the 1994 accident near Columbus, Ohio illustrate?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: concepts and context
o: Use: the pilot used the autopilot according to procedure and everything worked as designed
Abuse: the airline required pilots to use the autopilot in every phase of flight
Disuse: the pilot turned off the autopilot from distrust and flew manually for the whole flight
Misuse: a pilot with low confidence in manual skills relied heavily on the autopilot
mcq.e: The paper: "A pilot who demonstrated low confidence in his own manual control skills and tended to rely heavily on the automatic pilot during nighttime, low-visibility approaches failed to monitor the aircraft's airspeed".

mcq.q: What does the Strasbourg (Airbus A320) accident illustrate in the paper?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: concepts and context
o: Constant false alarms leading the crew to switch the whole system off
The difficulty of managing complex guidance modes: the crew apparently confused two modes
Pilots turning off all automated systems and flying by hand, causing loss of control
The autopilot accidentally giving a wrong directive that the pilots then followed blindly
mcq.e: The paper: "an Airbus A320 crashed in Strasbourg, France, when the crew apparently confused the vertical speed and flight path angle modes".

mcq.q: Wiener (1985, 1989) asked pilots about attitudes to automation. What was the notable finding?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: use (factors deciding use)
o: A large majority of pilots fully agreed that automation always greatly reduces workload
Only a minority of pilots agreed with the statement "automation reduces workload"
All pilots opposed introducing automation to the cockpit on safety grounds
Pilots had no opinion about workload and cared only about their pay
mcq.e: The paper: "only a minority of the pilots agreed with the statement, 'automation reduces workload.' In fact, a substantial minority of the pilots thought that automation had increased their workload."

mcq.q: What was a main source of increased workload according to later studies?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: use (factors deciding use)
o: Having to repair mechanical parts of the automation in flight
Having to talk with air traffic control more than before
Having to fill in post-flight report forms for the airline
Having to reprogram automated systems (such as the FMS) when conditions changed
mcq.e: The paper: "a major source of the increased workload was the requirement to reprogram automated systems such as the FMS when conditions changed (e.g., having to land at a different runway than originally planned)."

mcq.q: According to the paper, how do attitudes toward automation relate to actual reliance behavior?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: use (factors deciding use)
o: They are always opposed: whoever has a positive attitude often turns automation off
No researcher has ever looked at the question in any field
They always match completely: whoever has a positive attitude uses automation in all situations
They do not necessarily match: two studies found no relationship between attitudes and actual reliance
mcq.e: The paper: "Two recent studies found no relationship between attitudes toward automation and actual reliance on automation during multiple-task performance (Riley, 1994a, 1996; Singh et al., 1993b)."

mcq.q: Riley (1994a) manipulated tracking difficulty. What did he find about students' use of automation for the classification task?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: use (factors deciding use)
o: Students always used automation regardless of difficulty, at about 100% overall usage
The harder the task, the more students turned automation off, so nobody used it on hard trials
Difficulty did not affect the choice to use automation; overall usage was low, under about 50%
The harder the task, the more students used automation, reaching nearly 100% overall usage
mcq.e: The paper: "manipulating the difficulty of the tracking task had no impact on the students' choice to use automation in the classification task. The overall level of automation usage in this group was quite low—less than about 50%."

mcq.q: How does the paper explain operators often citing workload although the data are unclear?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: use (factors deciding use)
o: All pilots rate workload in the same way, so there are no individual differences
Operators often cite workload as a factor, but there are large individual differences
Operators never mention workload in any survey
Workload can always be measured accurately by instruments so users need not be asked
mcq.e: The paper: "human operators often cite excessive workload as a factor in their choice of automation... these data also showed substantial individual differences... very few gave an answer in the middle."

mcq.q: What is "cognitive overhead" in the paper?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: use (factors deciding use)
o: The monetary cost of buying and installing automation equipment in the cockpit
The workload associated with the decision to use the automation itself
The pilot's fatigue after a long flight caused by lack of sleep and long hours
The cost of training new pilots so that they are certified to operate automated systems
mcq.e: The paper: "a related form of workload—that associated with the decision to use the automation itself—may also influence automation use... the cognitive 'overhead' involved may persuade the operator not to use the automation".

mcq.q: Which everyday example does the paper use to illustrate cognitive overhead?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: use (factors deciding use)
o: Going to work by bus or on foot when it rains
Cooking with a microwave or on a traditional gas stove
Calling a friend or texting when you need to make urgent contact
Entering text from a sheet of paper: typing it manually or using a scanner and OCR program
mcq.e: The paper: "entering text from a sheet of paper into a word processor. One choice... is to enter the text manually with a keyboard. Alternatively, a scanner and an optical character recognition (OCR) program can be used".

mcq.q: What did Kirlik (1993) find with a Markov analysis?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: use (factors deciding use)
o: There are no conditions in which not using automation is reasonable
Participants always used automation exactly as its designer intended
There are conditions for which the optimal choice is not to use the automation
The optimal choice is always to use the automation under all conditions
mcq.e: The paper: "Using a Markov modeling analysis to identify the optimal strategies of automation use... he found that conditions exist for which the optimal choice is not to use the automation." In this study no participant used the autopilot as intended.

mcq.q: According to Muir (1988), what affects trust in machines?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: use (factors deciding use)
o: The same factors that affect trust between people: reliable and honest, lost when let down
The color and outside design of the machine rather than how well it performs
The price of the machine: the more expensive the machine, the more people trust it, however it performs
Factors wholly different from trust between people, because machines have no emotions or motives
mcq.e: The paper: "Muir (1988) argued that individuals' trust for machines can be affected by the same factors that influence trust between individuals; for example, people trust others if they are reliable and honest, but they lose trust when they are let down or betrayed, and the subsequent redevelopment of trust takes time."

mcq.q: When did Lee and Moray (1994) find that participants chose manual control?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: use (factors deciding use)
o: When their trust in the automation exceeded their confidence in their own ability
When workload was low and they had plenty of spare time while operating
When a supervisor gave a direct written order to switch to manual control
When their confidence in their own ability to control the plant exceeded their trust in the automation
mcq.e: The paper: "participants chose manual control if their confidence in their own ability to control the plant exceeded their trust of the automation, and that they otherwise chose automation."

mcq.q: What did Parasuraman et al. (1993) find after the simulated catastrophic failure of an automated engine-monitoring system?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: use (factors deciding use)
o: Participants switched it off at once and moved to manual control with excellent performance
Participants continued to rely on the automation for some time, though less than when it was more reliable
Participants immediately stopped using the automation and never used it again in the experiment
Participants did not notice the system had failed and kept relying on it as before
mcq.e: The paper: "even after the simulated catastrophic failure of an automated engine-monitoring system, participants continued to rely on the automation for some time, though to a lesser extent than when the automation was more reliable."

mcq.q: Why might occasional failures not reduce trust much, per the paper's explanations?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: use (factors deciding use)
o: If reliability is high, operators come to rely on it
Because users are always warned of a failure in advance and have a backup plan ready
Because users never notice the machine's failures under any circumstances
Because failures always happen at moments the user cannot notice
mcq.e: The paper: "if automation reliability is relatively high, then operators may come to rely on the automation, so that occasional failures do not substantially reduce trust in the automation unless the failures are sustained."

mcq.q: What did Riley (1994a) find about participants' self-confidence in their own skills?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: use (factors deciding use)
o: It was always well founded: they assessed their own performance accurately and used automation sensibly
It affected only pilots; students did not use self-confidence in their decisions at all
It was unrelated to the decision to use automation because they followed a fixed rule
It was not necessarily justified: they could not accurately assess their own performance to decide on using automation
mcq.e: The paper: "he did not find that self-confidence was necessarily justified; participants in his studies were not able to accurately assess their own performance and use the automation accordingly".

mcq.q: What is the paper's conclusion about predicting an individual's decision to use automation?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: use (factors deciding use)
o: It is hard to predict systematically because of the complex interaction of factors
It can be predicted perfectly from an attitude questionnaire alone
No prediction is needed because all operators decide in exactly the same way
It is easy to predict exactly if you know the operator's age and flight hours
mcq.e: The paper: "large individual differences make systematic prediction of automation use by specific operators difficult."

mcq.q: Since the use decision is hard to predict, what does the paper recommend for policies and procedures?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: use (factors deciding use)
o: Highlight the specific considerations to weigh when deciding to use automation rather than leaving the decision open to bias
Ban automation completely and force manual flying in every phase of flight
Leave each person to decide with no guidance or training whatsoever
Forbid operators from deciding and force them to use automation in every situation
mcq.e: The paper: "policies and procedures should highlight the importance of taking specific considerations into account when deciding whether or not to use automation, rather than leaving that decision vulnerable to biases and other factors that may result in suboptimal strategies."

mcq.q: Which two error types does "automation bias" lead to, per the paper?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: Communication errors and coordination errors when several people run a system
Omission errors (missing a problem because the aid did not flag it)
Calculation errors and typing errors when operators enter data into the system
Hardware errors and software errors when the machine deviates from its designer's plan
mcq.e: The paper: "Automation bias may result in omission errors, in which the operator fails to notice a problem or take an action because the automated aid fails to inform the operator... Commission errors occur when operators follow an automated directive that is inappropriate."

mcq.q: What did Mosier and colleagues find about pilots' use of automated cues?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: They always cross-checked every automated cue against at least three independent information sources
They used automated cues as a heuristic replacement for information seeking
They ignored automated cues completely and trusted only traditional mechanical gauges
They used automated cues only when directly ordered by air traffic control
mcq.e: The paper: "pilots tended to use automated cues as a heuristic replacement for information seeking... pilots tended not to use disconfirming evidence available from cockpit displays when there was a conflict between expected and actual automation performance."

mcq.q: What do similar automation bias error rates in students and professional pilots show?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: Neither group makes errors, so the bias hardly exists in practice
Students make far fewer errors because they are younger and have faster reflexes
Expertise does not guarantee immunity from this bias
Professional pilots make far fewer errors, so experience fully protects against the bias
mcq.e: The paper: "Automation bias error rates were also found to be similar for student and professional pilot samples, indicating that expertise does not guarantee immunity from this bias".

mcq.q: What does the paper say about human monitoring in general?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: Humans always monitor badly in every circumstance and this cannot be improved in any way
Humans always monitor perfectly in every circumstance and never make monitoring errors
Monitoring matters only in aviation and is unnecessary in other fields
It can be very efficient when the number of opportunities for failure is considered
mcq.e: The paper: "human monitoring can be very efficient... When the number of opportunities for failure is considered... the relatively low frequency of monitoring errors is striking... The absolute number of errors may be high, however".

mcq.q: What did Hilburn, Jorna and Parasuraman (1995) find for air traffic controllers using an automated descent advisor?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: They responded much more slowly to secondary malfunctions than in unaided performance
They responded identically in both conditions, so the tool had no effect
They responded faster to secondary malfunctions than in unaided performance
They responded to no secondary malfunctions during the whole simulation
mcq.e: The paper: "experienced controllers using an automated descent advisor were quicker to respond to secondary malfunctions (pilots not replying to data-linked clearances)."

mcq.q: In Parasuraman et al.'s studies, when did participants detect more than 70% of engine malfunctions?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: When engine monitoring was fully given to the machine under constant reliability
When a second person sat next to them reminding them to check the engine every minute
When they performed the engine monitoring task manually while also doing tracking
When they had nothing else to do but watch a screen for two hours
mcq.e: The paper: "Participants detected more than 70% of malfunctions on the engine status task when they performed the task manually while simultaneously carrying out tracking and fuel management. However, when the engine status task was under automation control, detection of malfunctions was markedly reduced in the constant reliability condition."

mcq.q: In the separate experiment with only the monitoring task (no tracking or fuel tasks), what was the detection rate of automation failures?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: About 70 percent, as when doing several tasks
About 20 percent, i.e., very low
Nearly perfect, above 95%
About 50 percent, i.e., at chance
mcq.e: The paper: "Individuals were now nearly perfect (> 95%) in detecting failures in the automated control of the engine status task, which was the only task."

mcq.q: What do these results (single task above 95%, multitask poor) show?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: Operators can be poor at monitoring automation when they must do other manual tasks at the same time: long-term automation has a potential cost
Humans cannot monitor machines at all, so human monitoring should be abandoned completely
Monitoring is poor only when the operator is tired and has nothing to do with the number of tasks
Automation never affects human monitoring however many tasks are done at once
mcq.e: The paper: "These results point to the potential cost of long-term automation on system performance and show that operators can be poor at monitoring automation when they have to perform other manual tasks simultaneously."

mcq.q: Which reliability condition produced better monitoring performance in Parasuraman et al. (1993)?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: The two conditions gave identical monitoring performance in every block
Variable reliability (switching low/high every 10 min) beat constant reliability
Only 100 percent reliability gave better monitoring than other conditions
Constant reliability beat variable reliability in every time block
mcq.e: The paper: "monitoring performance was significantly higher in the variable reliability condition than in the constant reliability condition."

mcq.q: How did detection of automation failures relate to automation reliability in May, Molloy and Parasuraman (1993)?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: Detection varied in the same direction as automation reliability
Detection varied inversely with automation reliability
Detection always equaled the automation's reliability
Detection was completely independent of automation reliability
mcq.e: The paper: "the detection rate of automation failures varied inversely with automation reliability."

mcq.q: What did Mosier et al. (1994) find in ASRS incidents where overreliance was suspected?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: 7% involved a probable monitoring failure
27% involved a probable monitoring failure
100% involved a probable monitoring failure
77% involved a probable monitoring failure
mcq.e: The paper: "Mosier et al. (1994) found that 77% of ASRS incidents in which overreliance on automation was suspected involved a probable failure in monitoring."

mcq.q: What does the Royal Majesty grounding illustrate?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: A satellite navigation system failed "silently" and the crew did not monitor other position sources
The designer blocked the crew from steering manually in an emergency
The satellite navigation gave constant false alarms so the crew switched it off for peace
The crew abandoned automatic navigation entirely and followed an old paper chart
mcq.e: The paper: "a satellite-based navigational system failed 'silently' in a cruise ship that ran aground off Nantucket Island. The crew did not monitor other sources of position information".

mcq.q: Why is automated monitoring (a machine monitoring a machine) not a general solution, per the paper?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: Because law forbids all automated monitors in aviation and process control
Because machine monitors are always less accurate than people in every kind of task
Because machine monitors are so expensive that no organization can buy one
It can increase the number of alarms and lead to infinite regress if another system monitors the automated monitor
mcq.e: The paper: "automated monitors can increase the number of alarms... to protect against failure of automated monitors, designers may be tempted to put in another system that monitors the automated monitor, a process that could lead to infinite regress."

mcq.q: How does the paper explain poor detection of automation failures when attention is elsewhere?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: Attentional rather than purely visual factors: centrally locating the automated task did not help
Purely visual factors: putting the automated task at the screen center always fully fixes it
Purely auditory factors: adding a sound alert always fully fixes it
Weather factors: it happens only on night flights and not by day
mcq.e: The paper: "Neither centrally locating the automated task... nor superimposing it on the primary manual task... mitigates this effect. These results suggest that attentional rather than purely visual factors... underlie poor monitoring."

mcq.q: What did the integrated EMACS display help with in Molloy and Parasuraman's work?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: Participants detected all automation failures with both displays
Participants detected less than half as many automation failures as with the non-integrated display
Participants detected twice as many automation failures as with the non-integrated display (about a third at baseline)
Participants detected exactly the same number of automation failures as with the non-integrated display
mcq.e: The paper: "participants detected only about a third of the automation failures with the nonintegrated baseline display, [and] they detected twice as many failures with the integrated EMACS display."

mcq.q: How was adaptive task allocation tested and what happened?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: Every 10 minutes the entire system was turned off for an hour to let the operator rest
Giving the task to the human for the whole 40 minutes improved monitoring but ruined tracking
Keeping the task fully automated for the whole experiment was the best way to improve monitoring
After 40 minutes of automation, giving the monitoring task back to the human for 10 minutes improved later monitoring
mcq.e: The paper: "after a 40-min period of automation, a 10-min period in which the task was reallocated to the operator had a beneficial impact on subsequent operator monitoring under automation."

mcq.q: What does "premature cognitive commitment" (Langer) describe in the paper?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: The operator promises the manager early that the task will be finished on time
The operator commits never to use the machine again after its first failure
The designer promises users early a launch date and features for the system
An operator who believes the automation is 100% reliable will hardly monitor its inputs or second-guess its outputs, which shapes later attitude
mcq.e: The paper: "The operator who believes that the automation is 100% reliable will be unlikely to monitor inputs to the automation or to second-guess its outputs. In Langer's (1989) terms, the human makes a 'premature cognitive commitment'".

mcq.q: What vicious circle involving manual skill does the paper describe?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: Manual skill is unrelated to reliance because the two factors are wholly separate
Little chance to practice manual skills leads to skill loss
Manual skill declines only in older people, while younger people always keep it
The more chance to practice manual skills, the more the operator relies on the machine
mcq.e: The paper: "the operator has little opportunity to practice the skills involved in performing the automated task manually. If this is the case, then the loss in the operator's own skills relative to the performance of the automation will tend to lead to an even greater reliance on the automation... creating a vicious circle."

mcq.q: What did Whitfield, Ball and Ord (1980) report for controllers using automated conflict resolutions?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: A loss of the "mental picture" of the traffic when they used automated resolutions under high workload
Controllers used automated resolutions only when traffic was light and there was no pressure
Controllers understood the traffic better with automated resolutions under high workload
Controllers never used automated resolutions because they did not trust them at all
mcq.e: The paper: "Whitfield, Ball, and Ord (1980) reported such a loss of the 'mental picture' in controllers, who tended to use automated conflict resolutions under conditions of high workload and time pressure."

mcq.q: Which strategies does the paper suggest to reduce overreliance?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: misuse (automation bias and monitoring)
o: Ban all automated systems and force operators to work manually in every situation
Increase the number of alarms so the operator must attend to every warning
Cut all feedback about automation state so the operator is not overloaded
Make state indications salient, require some active operator involvement
mcq.e: The paper: "ensuring that state indications are salient enough to draw operator attention, requiring some level of active operator involvement in the process, and ensuring that the other demands on operator attention do not encourage the operator to ignore the automated processes."

mcq.q: Which two factors determine a device's false alarm rate and hence operator trust?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: disuse and abuse
o: The value of the decision criterion and the base rate of the hazardous condition
The number of operators and their salaries in the using organization
The price of the device and the expected lifetime of the sensors in the system
The color of the alarm light and the volume of the warning buzzer in the cockpit
mcq.e: The paper: "Two important factors that influence the device false alarm rate and, hence, the operator's trust in an automated alerting system are the values of the decision criterion and the base rate of the hazardous condition."

mcq.q: For an alarm system with d′ = 4.7, hit rate .999, false alarm rate .0594 and base rate .001, what is the posterior probability of a true alarm?
mcq.sec: Parasuraman and Riley 1997: disuse and abuse
o: About .0168, i.e., 1 in 59 alarms is true
About .168, i.e., 1 in 6 alarms is true
About .68, i.e., 2 in 3 alarms are true
About .999, i.e., almost every alarm is true
mcq.e: The paper: "when the a priori probability (base rate) of a hazardous condition is low (say, .001), only 1 in 59 alarms that the system emits represents a true hazardous condition (posterior probability = .0168)."

mcq.q: What does the paper conclude from that Bayesian example?

Achieving this performance sometimes requires very complex algorithms that can be extremely hard to understand... there may be some circumstances in which making automation simpler but less capable outweighs the benefits of making it more complex and trustworthy but less trustable."

mcq.q: Why does the paper say completely trustworthy automation is unachievable?
mcq.sec: Lee and See 2004: design recommendations
o: Because of design errors, maintenance problems and unanticipated variability
Because users always resist and deliberately sabotage every automated system
Because law forbids perfect automated systems
Because the cost is too high to build a perfect system
mcq.e: The paper: "Design errors, maintenance problems, and unanticipated variability make completely reliable and trustworthy automation unachievable."

mcq.q: What can appropriate trust lead to for the joint human-automation system?
mcq.sec: Lee and See 2004: design recommendations
o: Performance that is always worse than the human alone
Performance that always exactly equals the automation alone
Performance that can be superior to either the human or the automation alone
No relation to the joint performance of the system
mcq.e: The paper: "Appropriate trust can lead to performance of the joint human-automation system that is superior to the performance of either the human or the automation alone (Sorkin & Woods, 1985; Wickens et al., 2000)."

mcq.q: Why does the paper say training should address gossip and informal discussion of the automation?
mcq.sec: Lee and See 2004: design recommendations
o: Because gossip tires operators, so all talk during work should be banned
Because gossip can pull operators' understanding away from true capability (e.g.
Because gossip is always more accurate than official data and should replace training material
Because gossip does not affect trust, so the paper mentions it only for completeness
mcq.e: The paper: "response times to warnings tend to increase when false alarms occur. This effect was counteracted by gossip that suggested that the rate of false alarms was lower than it actually was (Bliss, Dunn, & Fuller, 1995)" and recommends: "Gossip and informal discussion of automation capabilities need to be considered in training and retraining".

mcq.q: What is "meta trust" in the paper?
mcq.sec: Lee and See 2004: design recommendations
o: A machine's trust in the user when the user sends a command
A person's trust that another person's trust in the automation is appropriate
A manager's trust in the company's safety policy
A user's trust in the designer's own programming ability
mcq.e: The paper: "Meta trust refers to the trust a person has that the other person's trust in the automation is appropriate."

mcq.q: Why should the figures in the three papers (59%, 97%, 35%, reliability thresholds of 60-90%) not be applied directly to a programming class with AI?
mcq.sec: Interpretation, limits and thesis design
o: Because later studies on generative AI have proven the figures wrong
They come from simulations or specific systems (aviation, process control)
Because the figures hold only for pilots and students never behave similarly
Because the authors retracted the figures in later publications
mcq.e: All three papers come from aviation and process control; Skitka used the W/Panes simulation with students; the reliability threshold is described as "highly system and context dependent".

mcq.q: Which of the three papers is a single experiment?
mcq.sec: Interpretation, limits and thesis design
o: Skitka, Mosier and Burdick (1999)
All three are single experiments
Lee and See (2004)
Parasuraman and Riley (1997)
mcq.e: Parasuraman and Riley, and Lee and See, are reviews or conceptual frameworks; Skitka et al. report one simulation experiment with 80 students.

mcq.q: Why do the correlations in Skitka's Table 1 not prove causation?
mcq.sec: Interpretation, limits and thesis design
o: Because the correlations were computed on the unaided group, unrelated to commission errors
They are exploratory analyses in a sample of 40 AMA participants
Because they were verified by a separate randomized experiment
Because the correlations equal zero, so they show no relation between the variables
mcq.e: The paper: "Only the automated condition sample was used for these analyses" (N = 40) under "Exploratory analyses"; the belief and diffusion variables were questionnaire measures.

mcq.q: Do Skitka et al. say automation is bad?
mcq.sec: Interpretation, limits and thesis design
o: Yes: they conclude the aided group was always worse than the unaided group on every event
No: they conclude automation bias does not exist in the study context
No: when the AMA was right people did better; the cost appears when it is wrong or does not prompt
Yes: they recommend abandoning automated monitoring aids in every industry
mcq.e: The paper: "The goal in settings where errors can lead to catastrophic consequences will not be to avoid using automated decision aids because they may introduce a new class of errors, but instead to use automated monitoring devices where they seem to be indicated, and then to take steps to try to minimize the probability of errors related to automation bias."

mcq.q: In a thesis on AI teaching programming, how could "misuse" and "disuse" be measured (design inference)?
mcq.sec: Interpretation, limits and thesis design
o: Hours students use AI and hours they take breaks during class
The rate of accepting wrong AI answers or code
Final exam grade and attendance grade in the same semester
Lines of code students write and syntax errors the compiler reports in class
mcq.e: Design inference from the definitions of misuse (overreliance, accepting when one should not) and disuse (ignoring when one should use); the module's simulation computes both rates in a simplified model.

mcq.q: Why measure trust per AI function (specificity) instead of one general item (design inference)?
mcq.sec: Interpretation, limits and thesis design
o: Because one general question always gives more accurate results than several specific ones
Because students use AI for only one function, so functions need not be distinguished
Because trust can be function- and situation-specific; the AI may be strong at one task
Because many questions tire students, so ask as few as possible
mcq.e: Lee and See: functional specificity is the degree to which trust is tied to particular functions or modes; a fault in one controller did not reduce trust in independent controllers.

essay.q: Present and distinguish Parasuraman and Riley's (1997) four concepts: use, misuse, disuse and abuse. For each give one example from the paper and one implication for AI use in a programming class.
essay.m: Hint: Use: voluntary engaging/disengaging; Misuse: overreliance (Columbus 1994, failure to monitor); Disuse: ignoring or turning off alarms (Baltimore 1987, tape over buzzers); Abuse: designers/managers applying automation without regard for consequences for humans (weight-on-wheels sensor, Gaithersburg). Implications (design inference): misuse is accepting wrong AI code; disuse is rejecting right suggestions; abuse is designing a class that puts students in a passive monitor role; use is the decision to use AI and how.

essay.q: Explain the Bayesian false alarm example in Parasuraman and Riley (base rate .001, hit rate .999, false alarm .0594). Why can a sensitive system still be ignored? Give two remedies the paper suggests.
essay.m: Hint: Posterior probability .0168, i.e., 1 in 59 alarms is true, because of the low base rate. Operators "cry wolf" and ignore or disable alarms; Getty et al.: slower responses as true-alarm probability fell from .75 to .25; the prison escape example. Remedies: consider both threshold and base rate in design; multi-level "likelihood" alarms rather than final authority; consider the effect of false alarms on trust when setting performance requirements.

essay.q: Describe the design, main results and limits of Skitka, Mosier and Burdick's (1999) experiment. What can be generalized to classrooms and what cannot?
essay.m: Hint: 80 students; W/Panes; AMA group (told not fully reliable, other indicators 100% accurate) vs no-aid group; 6 omission opportunities (59% vs 97% correct), 6 commission opportunities (35% correct, no comparison group); on the other 88 events the AMA group was more correct; exploratory correlations (belief in AMA accuracy, diffusion of responsibility). Limits: simulation, students, correlation is not causation, generalization needs replication. Cautious generalization: the structure "good when the aid is right, worse when it is wrong"; do not generalize the specific numbers.

essay.q: Present Lee and See's (2004) concepts of calibration, resolution and specificity and the three bases performance, process and purpose. Propose how to measure two of them for students' trust in a programming AI.
essay.m: Hint: Calibration: match between trust and true capability (overtrust, distrust); resolution: differentiating capability levels; specificity: by function and over time. Performance (what it does), process (how it works), purpose (what it is for). Proposal (design inference): calibration by comparing item-level trust with the AI's actual accuracy on that item; specificity by separate trust scales for functions (explaining errors, generating code, suggesting algorithms); note the limits of self-report questionnaires.

essay.q: Describe the closed loop between trust and reliance in Lee and See's dynamic model. Why can trust be both fragile and durable, and what does this imply for designing an experiment on AI?
essay.m: Hint: Not using means little information so trust hardly grows; high trust means less monitoring so faults go unnoticed; inertia; sensitivity to initial experience and worst behavior; unpredictable faults hurt more than large constant ones; the threshold depends on the system. Implication (design inference): record the interaction history, consider the order of exposure (AI right first or wrong first) and measure trust at several time points rather than once.

essay.q: Drawing on all three papers, propose components of a "responsible AI" model for a programming class aimed at appropriate reliance, and state what must be tested empirically because the papers did not show it.
essay.m: Hint: From Lee and See: show past reliability and limits, explain the process, state purpose, design for appropriate trust; from Parasuraman and Riley: keep students in an active role, salient feedback, consider adaptive automation; from Skitka: teach recognition of the bias (verification prompts alone are not enough). Not shown: effects with generative AI and programming, long-term effects, whether these measures improve learning; these are hypotheses to be tested.
